text:
Parsnip.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Autumn / Winter

Parsnips are slow, deep-rooting biennials grown for white tap roots that sweeten as cold turns starch to sugar. They occupy the ground for a long season and seedlings emerge slowly, but established plants need little beyond weed control and moisture while young. Use fresh seed: cold or dry soil and sowing too deeply can leave a blank row. Deep, humus-rich, stone-free ground gives the best roots, preferably undug or improved for an earlier crop; avoid fresh manure.

Quick facts
Sow

Mar–Apr. Feb needs warm soil. May–early Jun gives smaller roots and may reduce canker.

Harvest

Oct – Apr

Germination

10–30 days

Sowing depth

1/2 in.

Row spacing

12 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

8 lb

Plant spacing

Thin to 6 in. apart.

Ready in

About 34 weeks from sowing

Recommended varieties
Gladiator

A well-established hybrid parsnip producing useful, even roots. A strong first choice for the main autumn and winter crop.

Tender and True

A traditional parsnip grown for long roots and good flavour. Keep as the familiar open-pollinated alternative.

Palace F1

An early-to-maincrop hybrid with smooth roots, shallow crowns and some canker resistance. A useful alternative to Gladiator.

Key risks
Canker

In wet winters, heavy soils, acid soil or ground containing fresh manure, the tops of roots may develop brown or black fungal rot.

Poor germination

Parsnip seed loses viability quickly.

Carrot root fly

Carrot fly larvae tunnel into parsnip roots, leaving rusty-brown scars and making damaged roots vulnerable to rot.

Forking

Forked roots are usually caused by stones, heavy soil, fresh manure, lumpy compost or ground that has not been improved deeply enough in advance.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
72
ROOT CROPS

Use fresh seed and sow in place.

Germination is slow; keep the seedbed moist while you wait.

Prepare for long, straight roots.

Avoid stones, compaction and fresh manure just before sowing.

Soil & preparation
Choose deep, friable, stone-free soil improved for a previous crop. Shorter varieties suit shallower or heavier ground.
Avoid fresh manure/lumpy compost. Rake clean; test acid soil before liming to pH 6.5.
Sowing & planting
Sow fresh seed
Thin in place
Sow 

Use fresh seed. Sow thinly or place three seeds at each spot, ½ in. deep. Cover with fine soil or compost, firm and keep moist. A few radish seeds can mark the slow-germinating row.

Looking after the crop
At each spot keep the strongest seedling. Discard the thinnings, as moving young parsnips disturbs the taproot.
Thin carefully, weed while seedlings are small and avoid disturbing crowns or roots.
Keep young plants moist: early checks reduce yield, although mature roots reach deep moisture. Mulch between rows with fine mature compost, especially on low-humus soil; keep crowns clear and stop weeds seeding.
Harvesting & storage
Lift useful roots from autumn; cold improves sweetness and dry weather can make lifting cleaner. Loosen deeply with a fork and ease out: pulling against firm ground snaps long tap roots.
Leave roots in the ground through winter where lifting remains practical. Lift a batch before hard freezes and store in damp sand, cool and frost-free.
Finish the crop before spring regrowth and flowering make roots woody.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Canker	Brown or black rot at root crowns.	Resistant varieties; avoid damage and fresh manure.
Poor germination	Seedlings fail to appear.	Use fresh seed; keep moist and resow while season allows.
Carrot root fly	Rusty-brown scars and tunnels in roots; damaged roots may rot.	Cover with insect-proof mesh from sowing; secure every edge.
Forking	Roots divide into several forks.	Remove stones; avoid compaction and fresh manure.
Leaf miner	Blistered leaf mines with maggots.	Tolerate light damage; remove badly mined leaf parts.
Sclerotinia rot	White woolly mould and soft rot.	Discard affected roots; keep stores clean and airy.
Violet root rot	Purplish felt-like threads coat roots.	Discard affected roots; avoid storing suspect roots.
Final tips

A few radishes mark slow-germinating rows and can be harvested before parsnips need the space.

Lift only what you need while winter soil remains workable; keep stored roots from drying out.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
